messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bao, a 31-year-old carpenter, described the past six months as living inside a pressure cooker with no release valve. The incident itself had been jarringly mundane at its start. He was driving home from a job site, his truck laden with tools and off-cuts of cedar, when he saw the flashing lights in his rearview mirror. He’d made an incomplete stop at a sign a few blocks back. But the routine traffic stop spiraled. The officer’s tone was aggressive, his questions rapid-fire. Confused and increasingly nervous, Bao fumbled for his registration. When a second officer appeared at his passenger-side window, unseen and unheard until he tapped on the glass, Bao flinched violently. That was all it took. He was pulled from the truck, slammed against the door, and cuffed. The delay, the sudden escalation from a minor mistake to physical force, the feeling of being trapped and unable to see the men behind him, had rewired his sense of safety.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to feel like a series of potential ambushes. Bao found he was unable to relax, even at home with his wife, Mai. A pervasive, humming anxiety settled deep in his bones. At his workshop, he rearranged his entire setup, moving his primary workbench so that it was flush against the back wall, allowing him an unobstructed view of the large bay door. He told his partner it was for better light, but the truth was he couldn't bear the thought of anyone walking in behind him. This constant, exhausting vigilance only intensified his belief that danger was imminent. When a lumber delivery was thirty minutes late, he didn't just feel impatient; he was consumed by a certainty that something terrible had happened—a catastrophic accident, a violent confrontation. He would call the supplier repeatedly, his heart pounding until he heard a dispatcher’s bored voice on the other end.

This relentless sense of threat became an intolerable state to live in. To manage the feeling of being constantly unsafe, Bao began turning inward, searching for a reason. He would spend hours replaying the traffic stop, convinced it was his fault. *If only I hadn’t flinched. If I had answered more clearly. If I had just found the papers faster.* This pattern of self-blame became a punishing, circular ritual he hoped would give him a sense of control, a rulebook for avoiding future disaster. When the rumination grew too loud, and the effort to avoid thinking about the event felt like holding a beach ball underwater, he started smoking cannabis before bed. It was the only thing that seemed to quiet the noise and blunt the edges of his hyper-awareness, allowing him a few hours of dreamless sleep.

But these strategies, meant to bring relief, only tightened the trap. The endless self-blame reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe, that a single misstep on his part could invite catastrophe. This belief left him feeling even more vulnerable and on guard than before. The cannabis that helped him sleep left him feeling foggy and slow the next morning, a cognitive haze that made him feel less capable of detecting and responding to danger, which in turn amplified his baseline anxiety and made it impossible to ever truly relax. His attempts to push the memory away only made it return with more force, ambushing him when he least expected it. The very things he was doing to feel safe were making the world feel infinitely more threatening.

The strain began to show everywhere. His focus at work was shot, and he’d made a costly measuring error on a set of custom cabinets. Mai was growing distant, frustrated by his inability to be present with her and worried by the cloying smell of smoke that now clung to his clothes most evenings. It was after a particularly sharp argument, where she told him she felt like she was living with a ghost, that Bao finally made an appointment. He came to therapy feeling exhausted and ashamed, terrified that he was losing his grip and would eventually push away the one person he had left to trust. More than anything, he wanted to feel like he could sit in his own living room, with his back to the door, and believe he was truly home.
